clue.text: Criminal boss — the first one died violently

indicators.note: the first letter of the word boss is taken, as the dash links it to boss

parts.note: one as the article a

indicators.note: something done violently is thrown about, so the letters of died are jumbled

explanation.surface: A crime boss's first henchman has met a violent death.
explanation.walkthrough: 'one' is the article A here, not the numeral I; 'violently' is the anagram signal for died.
explanation.definitionFit: A baddie is an informal word for a villain or wrongdoer, so a criminal fits.

clue.text: Recite Farewell, My Lovely from memory

indicators.note: to recite is to say out loud, so the word for farewell counts only for how it is spoken

parts.note: bye is a casual farewell
heart, as in sweetheart, is a term of endearment like my lovely

explanation.surface: Someone is asked to recite the Raymond Chandler novel Farewell, My Lovely without the book.
explanation.walkthrough: Farewell, My Lovely is a Philip Marlowe novel by Raymond Chandler, matching the puzzle's crime-fiction theme.
explanation.definitionFit: Learning something so you can repeat it without notes is knowing it from memory, the same idiom.

clue.text: US lawman conceals memory of tragedy?

indicators.note: a thing that conceals another holds it inside, so the lawman's letters wrap round the memory

parts.note: a DA is a district attorney, a US prosecutor
RAM is random-access computer memory

explanation.surface: An American prosecutor hides a tragic recollection.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark shows that tragedy is one example of the wider category.
explanation.definitionFit: Tragedy is one genre of stage play, so it is an example of the wider category of theatre.

clue.text: If man performs evil acts, charge him — leaders included

definitions.text: If man performs evil acts, charge him — leaders included

indicators.note: the leaders are the opening letters of each word, and they are to be included one after another

explanation.surface: A rule: a wrongdoing official, even one at the top, should be formally accused.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines too: charging a wrongdoer, leaders included, is what a parliament does to a president.
explanation.definitionFit: Formally accusing a public official, even a head of state, of misconduct is the process the clue describes.

clue.text: Gang joined by Italian-American stripper?

parts.note: a mob is a criminal gang
US is short for American, as in the United States

explanation.surface: A mob is joined by an Italian-American exotic dancer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stripper?' is playful: the Möbius strip is a loop with a single side.
explanation.definitionFit: A Möbius strip is the one-sided band of paper, so the name is jokingly one who goes with a strip.

clue.text: Menacing suggestion: loser beaten up with rifle butt

indicators.note: something beaten up is knocked out of shape, so the letters of loser are rearranged
the butt is the end of a rifle, so the word's last letter is taken

explanation.surface: A thug threatens a loser by hitting him with a rifle butt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beaten up' turns LOSER into ORELS, then 'butt' gives E, the end of rifle.
explanation.definitionFit: Tacked onto a demand, this phrase hints at unpleasant consequences, a threat left unspoken.

clue.text: Prohibition: having three in charge

indicators.note: one piece is placed in the middle of the other here

parts.note: to indict is to charge formally with a crime
ter is Latin for three times, as in musical or prescription use

explanation.surface: A ban is imposed by a committee of three in charge.
explanation.walkthrough: TER is the Latin word for thrice.
explanation.definitionFit: An interdict is a formal ban or legal prohibition, especially in Scots law or the church.

clue.text: "Pole lifted stolen goods" — that's an informer

parts.note: S is the south pole

indicators.note: in a down clue, lifted means the word is raised, so it reads from the bottom up

parts.note: loot is stolen goods
i.e. is short for id est, that is

explanation.surface: A quote about a Polish man who lifted stolen goods, followed by a remark that he grassed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lifted' looks like stealing but reverses LOOT to TOOL; Pole is not a person but S.
explanation.definitionFit: Stoolie, from stool pigeon, is American slang for someone who tips off the police.

clue.text: Examine local yokels — to put through the wringer

indicators.note: clothes put through a wringer are squeezed and twisted, so these letters are mangled into a new order

explanation.surface: Detectives examine the village locals before giving them a hard grilling.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram uses every letter of LOCAL YOKELS TO.
explanation.definitionFit: To scrutinise something carefully is to examine it, a direct synonym phrase.

clue.text: Call to stop lying in new hoax

indicators.note: the letters are lying inside the words new hoax

explanation.surface: A demand to stop lying in a fresh deception.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lying' looks like telling untruths but means sitting inside the text.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the shout used to halt a horse, or anyone, a direct order to stop.

clue.text: Helping or turning back detective taken in by this criminal racket

indicators.note: the detective is taken in, enclosed by the other letters
the word or inside the helping is turned to face back the other way

parts.note: a portion is a helping of food
tec is short for detective

explanation.surface: A detective is helping or switching sides, absorbed into a criminal gang.
explanation.walkthrough: 'or turning back' reverses only the OR inside the helping, giving PROTION, before 'taken in by' encloses the detective.
explanation.definitionFit: A protection racket extorts money in return for sparing a business from harm.

clue.text: Tomorrow, exchange money for Bahamas' foremost fruit

indicators.note: to exchange one thing for another is to swap it, so one letter replaces another

parts.note: mañana is Spanish for tomorrow
M is an abbreviation for money, as in economists' M0, M1

indicators.note: the foremost part of Bahamas' is its first letter

explanation.surface: Tomorrow someone will change their money for the Caribbean's best fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'exchange' swaps the M (money) in MANANA for B, the first of Bahamas'.
explanation.definitionFit: The banana is a long yellow tropical fruit grown widely in the Caribbean.

clue.text: Hunters, winging it in battered deerstalkers, dare to go out

indicators.note: a battered thing is knocked out of shape, so the letters are rearranged
the letters of dare are to go out, removed from the jumble

explanation.surface: Huntsmen in tatty deerstalker hats dare to venture out and improvise.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove D, A, R, E from DEERSTALKERS and 'battered' rearranges the remaining ESTLKERS. A deerstalker is a cloth hunting cap, famously Sherlock Holmes's.
explanation.definitionFit: These small falcons hunt on the wing, hovering, so they are hunters that are flying.

clue.text: Part of gun detective loses points to a Scandinavian location

parts.note: the stock is the shoulder end of a gun

indicators.note: the detective loses some letters, which are taken away

parts.note: Sherlock Holmes is the fictional detective
E and S are compass points, east and south

explanation.surface: A detective drops some points to a Scandinavian place, with a gun part in play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'loses' drops E and S (compass points) from HOLMES.
explanation.definitionFit: Stockholm is the capital city of Sweden, a Scandinavian country.

clue.text: 26 perhaps the result of acid attack on hotshot in California

indicators.note: these letters go in, inside the state's abbreviation

parts.note: CA is the postal code for California

indicators.note: in a down clue, on means placed above the next piece

parts.note: rust is corrosion, the kind of damage acid does to metal
an ace is an expert or hotshot

explanation.surface: A grim news line: the outcome of an acid attack on a Californian star.
explanation.walkthrough: 26 is SCAMPI; 'perhaps' marks them as one example of the class.
explanation.definitionFit: Scampi are langoustines, members of the class of shelled arthropods including crabs and lobsters.

clue.text: Eat into racket with threats at its core

parts.note: a din is a loud racket

indicators.note: the core of a word is its middle letter

explanation.surface: Racketeers eat into a protection racket backed by threats.
explanation.walkthrough: 'racket' is noise here, not a criminal scheme.
explanation.definitionFit: To dine is to eat a meal, a direct synonym.

clue.text: Fight roughly, getting head knocked off

indicators.note: the word loses its first letter, its head

parts.note: about means roughly, approximately

explanation.surface: A rough fight in which someone's head is knocked off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'roughly' looks like how the fight goes but is the synonym ABOUT.
explanation.definitionFit: A bout is a boxing or wrestling contest, a single fight.

clue.text: Criminal libel: "US thugs"

indicators.note: something criminal is bent, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A tabloid headline commits criminal libel by calling Americans thugs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Criminal' looks like the definition but signals the anagram of LIBEL and US.
explanation.definitionFit: Bullies intimidate weaker people with force, like thugs or heavies.

clue.text: After a dispute, subdue with sweetener

indicators.note: subdue comes after a dispute in the answer

parts.note: to spar is to argue or dispute
to tame is to subdue

explanation.surface: Following an argument, someone calms things with a sweetener, perhaps a bribe.
explanation.definitionFit: Aspartame is an artificial low-calorie sugar substitute used in drinks.

clue.text: Where organised crime penetrated society that rejected drink

indicators.note: one piece penetrates the other, getting inside it

parts.note: AA is Alcoholics Anonymous, a fellowship of people giving up alcohol

indicators.note: organised means arranged, so the letters of crime are rearranged

explanation.surface: A history: organised crime got into a society that banned alcohol, the Prohibition era.
explanation.walkthrough: 'organised crime' reads as a single phrase but 'organised' is the anagram signal, giving MERIC. Alcoholics Anonymous is the society.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue describes the United States during Prohibition, so Where points to that country.

clue.text: Tough guy who investigated more lawbreaking

indicators.note: breaking the words smashes their letters into a new order

explanation.surface: A hard-boiled detective who looked into more crime.
explanation.walkthrough: The single word 'lawbreaking' is split in two: its first part is fodder and 'breaking' signals the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: Philip Marlowe is Raymond Chandler's hard-boiled private eye, a tough detective.

clue.text: Not exactly The Big Sleep, taking DNA in abduction case

indicators.note: the sleep is taking in other letters, so they go inside it
with taking, says the other letters go into the sleep

parts.note: a kip is a short sleep, so not a big one; The Big Sleep is a Chandler novel

explanation.surface: A crime story, unlike The Big Sleep, where DNA evidence is taken in an abduction.
explanation.walkthrough: KIP is British slang for a nap.
explanation.definitionFit: A kidnap is the seizing and holding of a person, so it is an abduction case.

clue.text: Fixed charge for flycatcher

parts.note: a flat rate or fee is a fixed one
a bill is a charge for goods or services

explanation.surface: A fixed fee is charged for a fly-catching service.
explanation.definitionFit: Flatbills are tropical American birds of the tyrant flycatcher family, named for their broad beaks.

clue.text: Of late, wrong to demand with menaces

parts.note: ex means former, from not long ago
a tort is a civil wrong in law

explanation.surface: Recently it has become wrong to make threatening demands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'demand with menaces' is the legal wording for blackmail.
explanation.definitionFit: To obtain money by threats is to blackmail, the legal phrase used in Britain.

clue.text: Gang gets time over botched raid

indicators.note: in a down clue, over means placed above the next piece
a botched job is messed up, so the letters of raid are rearranged

explanation.surface: Gang members are jailed after a failed robbery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gets time' looks like a prison sentence but gives T; 'botched' rearranges RAID.
explanation.definitionFit: A triad is a Chinese organised-crime syndicate, a gang.

clue.text: Here in Ohio, crime reported twice (returning thanks, Boatman)

indicators.note: reported speech is heard, so the doubled crime counts for how it is spoken
the word for crime is said two times over

parts.note: a sin is a wrongdoing, here said two times running

indicators.note: returning means the word for thanks is read backwards

parts.note: ta is British informal for thanks
the setter, Boatman, refers to himself as I

explanation.surface: A local says crime here in Ohio is reported twice over, and the setter offers thanks.
explanation.walkthrough: SIN SIN said aloud gives CINCINN; TA is reversed to AT.
explanation.definitionFit: Cincinnati is a major city in southwestern Ohio, on the Ohio River.

clue.text: Sarcasm not unknown as a weapon in the US

indicators.note: not means the unknown letter is taken away from the word

parts.note: irony is close to sarcasm, saying the opposite of what you mean
y is a mathematical unknown

explanation.surface: An observation that sarcasm, in America, can be used as a weapon.
explanation.definitionFit: Iron is American slang for a handgun, a gun or shooter.

clue.text: Detective on racket: "It's fishy"

indicators.note: in an across clue, the detective is put on after the racket

parts.note: a scam is a fraudulent racket
PI is a private investigator

explanation.surface: A detective investigating a swindle says it smells suspicious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fishy' looks like suspicion but describes seafood.
explanation.definitionFit: Scampi is breaded langoustine, a seafood dish, so it is literally fish-like food.

clue.text: Deal with body of crime writer

indicators.note: the body is everything but the extremities, so the first and last letters go

parts.note: Raymond Chandler wrote hard-boiled crime novels

explanation.surface: A literary agent deals with the corpse of a crime author.
explanation.walkthrough: 'body' looks like a corpse but means the writer's name without its ends.
explanation.definitionFit: To manage or cope with a situation is to tackle it, a direct synonym.
